newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia stocks plunge on Dow, new lending limits.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia stocks plunge on Dow, new lending limits.

text.p: Malaysia's share market slid further on Friday with brokerages making cash calls on their customers after prices dropped six percent during the week.
The market has been hit this week by sharp drops in U.S. share prices and central bank curbs on lending for property and stock purchases, the hottest sectors in Malaysia's booming economy.
By 2.35 p.m. local time (0635 GMT), the benchmark Composite Index had dropped 31.69 points to 1,120.823.61, or 2.75 percent on the day.
"The market is concerned about margin calls at the moment," said Soh Meng Hui, head of research at K.L. City Securities.
"There are some bad rumours of some stockbroking houses where punters have not been able to top up their margin calls, and have been forced to sell."
New York's Dow Jones industrial average set the bearish tone at the opening bell in Kuala Lumpur, having fallen 39.66 points on Thursday to close at 6477.35.
Key banking, stock brokerage and property issues were among the biggest losers.
Bank Negara's new guidelines, which took effect on April 1, limit financial institutions' lending to the property sector to no more than 20 percent of their total outstanding loans.

The central bank said it was maintaining a restriction on lending to finance purchases of stocks and mutual funds to 15 percent of an institution's portfolio and imposed new curbs on using shares as collateral to buy other shares.
In its annual report released last week, Bank Negara said it was concerned about speculative lending destabilising the banking system.

"The Bank's concern is predicated on the lessons of the last recession in the mid-1980s, as well as recent developments in the region," Central Bank Governor Ahmad Mohamed Don said in a preface to the report.

The banking system's exposure to the broad property sector stood at 95.5 billion ringgit at end-1996 or about 28.2 percent of total loans. Lending to the sector expanded by 30.5 percent in 1996, the report said.
Lending by the banking system for the purchase of shares increased 20.1 percent in 1996 to 26.1 billion, it said.
The market remained uncertain about how the measures will work and the confusion was weighing on share prices, market players said.
Bank Negara called a meeting of chief executives of financial institutions and brokerages on Thursday asking them to submit plans by April 15 on how they will comply with the new lending curbs.
"There is still confusion about what Bank Negara is going to do. There will be this uncertainty until there is something more clear," said Soh.

Foreigners were unloading Malaysian shares on Friday, brokers said, with conglomerate Sime Darby among the hardest hit. On Friday at midday Sime Darby's share price slipped five cents to 8.15 ringgit in active trading.
"There's some buying from local institutions, but the (selling) pressure is still there. The foreigners are looking at what stocks to sell, and they are targetting the blue chips," said Soh.
"People are averaging down (buying stocks as they fall), waiting for the bottom, but we just do not know where that is," said a dealer at a retail-based brokerage house.
"I think the selling is slightly overdone at the moment," he added.
